speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) how many Police reports have been made in 2023 and 2024 regarding fraudulent or counterfeit merchandise sold on e-commerce platforms where the seller and buyer were both in Singapore; (b) what were the considerations for such cases being deemed as commercial disputes rather than instances of cheating or scams; and (c) what recourse is available for affected buyers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Buyers who encounter allegedly counterfeit merchandise can file a Police report.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She said she filed a Police report, having purchased branded merchandise from a seller through the platform Carousell.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She says the seller claimed the merchandise was genuine but it turned out the merchandise was counterfeit.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My resident filed a Police report and was advised that the case was more of a contractual dispute and was referred to CASE.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: CASE told my resident it could not assist because the matter was between two private transactors.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, my resident is now wondering what redress might be possible in such situations, especially since she is of limited means and may find it hard to take up a case in the Courts?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Member had shared that his resident has faced difficulties seeking remedy through CASE.
